label: The physical design flow
prereqs: What a process design kit contains
lesson:
# The physical design flow

Physical design turns a gate-level netlist into geometry. Floorplanning fixes the chip outline, the core, the rows, the macros and the I/O; placement gives every standard cell a legal location; clock tree synthesis buffers the clock to the placed flip-flops; routing draws the wires. Placement sits in the middle, and a tool designer cares because its decisions set the wirelength, timing, congestion and power that every later stage inherits and can only partly repair.

## Floorplan, place, clock, route

The physical flow runs in a fixed order because each step needs the previous one's output. Floorplanning decides the die and core size, cuts the core into rows of sites, places the large macros (memories, analog blocks), assigns I/O pins and plans the power grid. Placement then works inside that region: it reads the netlist, the cell abstracts and the floorplan, and writes a location and orientation for every standard cell. Clock tree synthesis needs those locations, because it builds a buffered tree to the flip-flops where they now sit. Routing needs everything fixed, because it draws real metal between real pins. In OpenROAD these are separate engines over one database: floorplan and pin placement, global placement (gpl), detailed placement (dpl), CTS and global and detailed routing.

## Global, legal, detailed

Placement itself has three phases. Global placement treats cells as points or small blobs, minimises an estimate of wirelength and spreads cells so that no region is over-full, but tolerates overlap. Legalization snaps every cell into a row, aligns it to the site grid and removes all overlap with as little movement as possible. Detailed placement then improves the legal result with local moves: swapping cells, reordering short windows of a row, or matching groups of cells to slots. The split exists because the global problem is a huge continuous optimisation that is tractable only when legality is relaxed, while legality is a discrete, local property that is cheap to restore once cells are roughly in place. Wirelength is the main objective because it is fast to evaluate and correlates with wire capacitance, delay, power and routing demand.

## Why placement mistakes propagate

Placement is NP-hard even for wirelength alone, since it contains problems such as graph partitioning and minimum linear arrangement, so every placer is a heuristic and its errors flow downstream. Cells packed too tightly around a group of highly connected logic leave the router too few tracks, and the router reports overflow that it cannot fix without moving cells. Critical nets stretched by a wirelength-only objective fail timing, and CTS and routing can recover only a little with buffers and layer choices. A poor floorplan constrains the placer before it starts: if macros cut the rows into slivers or point their pins away from their logic, no placer can produce short nets. A tool designer therefore builds feedback into the placer: density targets, timing weights and congestion estimates that approximate what later stages will see.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapters 1 and 4; the OpenROAD project documentation for its flow.

problems.q:
Placement is commonly split into three phases. Which ordering is right?

A) Global placement, legalization, detailed placement

B) Legalization, global placement, detailed placement

C) Global placement, detailed placement, legalization

D) Detailed placement, global placement, legalization
problems.a: Global placement, legalization, detailed placement
problems.e: Global placement spreads cells roughly, legalization snaps them to rows and sites without overlap, and detailed placement improves the legal result locally.

problems.q:
What does placement take as input that floorplanning produced?

A) The clock tree and its skew targets

B) The routed nets and their parasitics

C) The gate-level netlist's logic function only

D) The core area, rows, fixed macros, I/O pins and placement blockages
problems.a: The core area, rows, fixed macros, I/O pins and placement blockages
problems.e: Placement works inside the region the floorplan defined, around the macros and pins it fixed.

problems.q:
In a standard RTL-to-GDSII flow, which order of physical-design steps is typical?

A) Routing, placement, clock tree synthesis, floorplanning

B) Placement, floorplanning, routing, clock tree synthesis

C) Floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing

D) Clock tree synthesis, floorplanning, routing, placement
problems.a: Floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing
problems.e: The floorplan fixes the region and macros, placement puts the cells, CTS builds the clock network on placed flops, and routing wires everything.

problems.q:
Why does a placer optimise wirelength when the real targets are timing, power and routability?

A) Wirelength is the only metric signoff checks

B) Timing does not depend on placement

C) Wirelength is cheap to compute and correlates with wire delay, wire capacitance and routing demand

D) Routers cannot route long wires at all
problems.a: Wirelength is cheap to compute and correlates with wire delay, wire capacitance and routing demand
problems.e: Shorter wires mean less capacitance, less delay and less routing demand, and HPWL can be evaluated millions of times per second.

problems.q:
A global placer ignores overlap between cells for most of its run. Why is that acceptable?

A) Overlap does not change wirelength

B) The router resolves overlaps

C) Legalization removes overlap afterwards, and a smooth overlap-tolerant model is far easier to optimise

D) Overlapping cells are legal in the final layout
problems.a: Legalization removes overlap afterwards, and a smooth overlap-tolerant model is far easier to optimise
problems.e: Global placement trades exact legality for a tractable continuous problem; legalization restores the invariant with small moves.

problems.q:
Which open-source flow runs floorplanning, placement (gpl and dpl), CTS and routing in one database?

A) OpenROAD

B) Verilator

C) ngspice

D) Yosys
problems.a: OpenROAD
problems.e: OpenROAD integrates the physical-design engines over one database; Yosys is synthesis, ngspice is circuit simulation and Verilator is RTL simulation.

problems.q:
Placement looks clean, but the router later reports thousands of overflowing edges in one region. Which earlier decision most likely caused it?

A) Cells were packed too densely in that region, leaving too few routing tracks for their nets

B) The netlist had too many inverters

C) The DEF units were too fine

D) The clock period was too short
problems.a: Cells were packed too densely in that region, leaving too few routing tracks for their nets
problems.e: Wirelength-driven placement can cluster highly connected logic; routing demand there exceeds supply. Routability-driven placement and density targets address it.

problems.q:
What is the main reason placement is NP-hard even for wirelength alone?

A) The number of rows is unbounded

B) HPWL has no closed form

C) It contains hard combinatorial problems such as minimum linear arrangement and graph partitioning as special cases

D) Cells have different widths only in theory
problems.a: It contains hard combinatorial problems such as minimum linear arrangement and graph partitioning as special cases
problems.e: Placing cells in slots to minimise connection length generalises NP-hard arrangement and partitioning problems, so practical placers use relaxations and heuristics.

problems.q:
After placement the timing report shows a long net on the critical path. Which step can still shorten it cheaply?

A) Timing-driven detailed placement or buffering before routing

B) Shrinking the die after routing

C) Changing the DEF database units

D) Re-running logic synthesis from RTL only
problems.a: Timing-driven detailed placement or buffering before routing
problems.e: Local placement moves and repeaters fix a long net without restarting the flow; later stages have less freedom.

label: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# Rows, sites and the placement region

Standard cells are not placed anywhere on the die. They sit in horizontal rows inside the core, each row divided into sites, the smallest legal horizontal step. This grid is what makes millions of cells abut cleanly and share power rails, and it is the discrete space that legalization and detailed placement work in. A tool designer must count it, index it and respect it exactly.

## Die, core, rows and sites

The die is the whole chip; the core is the inner region reserved for standard cells and macros, surrounded by the I/O ring or pad area. The core is filled with rows of equal height, the cell height of the library, for example 1.4 um in a 45 nm teaching library or 2.72 um for the SkyWater 130 nm high-density cells. Every standard cell has that height and a width that is an integer number of sites, the site being defined in the technology LEF (0.19 um wide in the 45 nm example, 0.46 um in sky130). Each row starts at an origin, has a site type and a count of sites, and an orientation. Cells in a row share a VDD rail along one edge and a VSS rail along the other, so they connect to power just by abutting.

## Counting rows and sites

With row height $h$ and site width $s$, a core of height $H$ holds $\lfloor H/h \rfloor$ rows and a row of width $W$ holds $\lfloor W/s \rfloor$ sites. A core 140.5 um tall with 1.4 um rows holds $\lfloor 140.5/1.4 \rfloor = 100$ rows, with 0.1 um left over at the top. If the core is 190.1 um wide and sites are 0.19 um, each row holds 1000 sites, and the core holds 100000 sites. A design of 15000 cells averaging 4 sites wide uses 60000 of them, a site utilization of 60%. Floorplanners usually choose the core size so the leftover is zero, but counting with floors is the safe habit, since a partial row or site cannot hold a cell.

## Rows as the legality grid

The rows and sites are the coordinate system of legality. A legal standard cell has its bottom edge on a row boundary, its left edge on a site boundary, and an orientation that matches the row: rows alternate between N and FS (flipped about the horizontal axis) so that the VDD rail of one row coincides with the VDD rail of the next. This makes legalization a discrete problem, an assignment of cells to row and site slots, and it lets a placer store a row as an ordered list of cells with integer site positions. It also defines what the global placer must approximate: a target density below 100% of the sites leaves room for buffers inserted later, for filler and tap cells, and for routing. Rows can be cut by macros and blockages, so a real row is a list of usable segments, not one interval.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 3 on chip planning and chapter 4 on placement; the LEF/DEF Language Reference for the SITE and ROW statements.

problems.q: A standard-cell library has a site 0.17 um wide and rows 1.2 um tall. The core region is 71.425 um wide and 50.547 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. How many complete placement rows fit in the core?
problems.e: Rows = floor(50.547 / 1.2) = 42. The leftover 0.147 um at the top cannot hold a full row.

problems.q: A standard-cell library has a site 0.46 um wide and rows 2.72 um tall. The core region is 198.123 um wide and 119.285 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. How many complete placement rows fit in the core?
problems.e: Rows = floor(119.285 / 2.72) = 43. The leftover 2.325 um at the top cannot hold a full row.

problems.q: A standard-cell library has a site 0.054 um wide and rows 0.27 um tall. The core region is 18.194 um wide and 20.928 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. How many complete placement rows fit in the core?
problems.e: Rows = floor(20.928 / 0.27) = 77. The leftover 0.138 um at the top cannot hold a full row.

problems.q: A standard-cell library has a site 0.38 um wide and rows 2.8 um tall. The core region is 66.104 um wide and 78.425 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. Each row is filled with whole sites from the left edge. How many sites does the whole core hold?

A standard-cell library has a site 0.46 um wide and rows 2.72 um tall. The core region is 182.04 um wide and 131.113 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. Each row is filled with whole sites from the left edge. How many sites does the whole core hold?

A standard-cell library has a site 0.17 um wide and rows 1.2 um tall. The core region is 117.397 um wide and 34.502 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. Each row is filled with whole sites from the left edge. How many sites does the whole core hold?

A standard-cell library has a site 0.2 um wide and rows 1.6 um tall. The core region is 52.161 um wide and 96.51 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. The netlist holds 1493 cells, each 7 sites wide. What percentage of the core's sites do they occupy? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Rows = 60 and sites per row = floor(52.161 / 0.2) = 260, so the core has 15600 sites. The cells need 1493 x 7 = 10451 sites, which is 67%.

problems.q: A standard-cell library has a site 0.054 um wide and rows 0.27 um tall. The core region is 32.513 um wide and 10.475 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. The netlist holds 3522 cells, each 5 sites wide. What percentage of the core's sites do they occupy? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Rows = 38 and sites per row = floor(32.513 / 0.054) = 602, so the core has 22876 sites. The cells need 3522 x 5 = 17610 sites, which is 77%.

problems.q: A standard-cell library has a site 0.19 um wide and rows 1.4 um tall. The core region is 64.002 um wide and 198.463 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. The netlist holds 2803 cells, each 12 sites wide. What percentage of the core's sites do they occupy? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Rows = 141 and sites per row = floor(64.002 / 0.19) = 336, so the core has 47376 sites. The cells need 2803 x 12 = 33636 sites, which is 71%.

label: Core utilization, aspect ratio and die size
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# Core utilization, aspect ratio and die size

Before any cell is placed, the floorplan must decide how big the core is. Too small and the cells do not fit or cannot be routed; too large and the wires grow long and the die costs more. Core utilization, aspect ratio and the I/O margin turn the netlist's total cell area into a concrete core and die rectangle, and every placer and router inherits that choice.

## Utilization from cell area

Core utilization is the total standard-cell area divided by the core area. Designers choose a target, commonly somewhere around 50% to 80%, leaving whitespace for routing, buffers added during optimisation, clock tree cells, tap and filler cells. The required core area is the cell area divided by the target: 200000 um$^2$ of cells at 70% utilization needs $200000/0.7 \approx 285714.3$ um$^2$ of core. Macros are usually counted separately, by adding their area plus halos to the core. The target is a trade-off: higher utilization shortens wires and shrinks the die, while lower utilization eases routing and timing closure. A placer's own target density is a local version of the same idea, applied bin by bin.

## Aspect ratio and core dimensions

The aspect ratio fixes the shape: with ratio $R = H/W$ and area $A$, the core width is $W = \sqrt{A/R}$ and the height is $H = RW$. For $A = 285714.3$ um$^2$ and $R = 1$, both are about 534.5 um. For $R = 2$ the core is $\sqrt{285714.3/2} \approx 378.0$ um wide and 756.0 um tall. In practice the height is then rounded to a whole number of rows and the width to a whole number of sites. Square cores minimise the average Manhattan distance between random points and are the default; other ratios follow from the package, from neighbouring blocks in a hierarchical design or from the shape of large macros.

## From core to die

The die adds a margin around the core for the I/O ring, pad cells or bumps, power rings and seal ring. With a uniform margin $m$, the die is $(W + 2m)(H + 2m)$. A 534.5 um square core with a 20 um margin gives a die about 574.5 um on a side, 330050 um$^2$. Small blocks pay heavily for the margin: a 100 um core with the same margin loses about 31% of its die area to it. Because die area drives cost and yield, while utilization drives routability, an agent tuning a floorplan treats utilization, aspect ratio and margin as Tier 1 parameters and measures their effect with a fast placement and congestion estimate before committing.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 3; the OpenROAD documentation for initialize_floorplan, which takes utilization, aspect ratio and core margins.

problems.q: The standard cells of a block have a total area of 27000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 70%. What core area is needed, in um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Utilization is cell area over core area, so the core is 27000 / 0.7 = 38571.4 um^2.

problems.q: The standard cells of a block have a total area of 199000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 65%. What core area is needed, in um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Utilization is cell area over core area, so the core is 199000 / 0.65 = 306153.8 um^2.

problems.q: The standard cells of a block have a total area of 58000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 75%. What core area is needed, in um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Utilization is cell area over core area, so the core is 58000 / 0.75 = 77333.3 um^2.

problems.q: The standard cells of a block have a total area of 141000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 80%. The core's aspect ratio (height over width) is 2. What is the core width, in um? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Core area = 141000 / 0.8 = 176250 um^2. With H = 2 W, the area is 2 W^2, so W = sqrt(176250 / 2) = 296.86 um.

problems.q: The standard cells of a block have a total area of 90000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 50%. The core's aspect ratio (height over width) is 0.75. What is the core width, in um? Round to 2 decimal places.

The standard cells of a block have a total area of 195000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 55%. The core's aspect ratio (height over width) is 0.75. What is the core width, in um? Round to 2 decimal places.

The standard cells of a block have a total area of 33000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 80%. The core has aspect ratio (height over width) 0.75, and the die adds an I/O margin of 24 um on every side of the core. What is the die area, in um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Core area 41250 um^2 with H/W = 0.75 gives W = 234.521 um and H = 175.891 um. The die is (W + 48)(H + 48) = 63253.7 um^2.

problems.q: The standard cells of a block have a total area of 264000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 75%. The core has aspect ratio (height over width) 2, and the die adds an I/O margin of 20 um on every side of the core. What is the die area, in um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Core area 352000 um^2 with H/W = 2 gives W = 419.524 um and H = 839.047 um. The die is (W + 40)(H + 40) = 403942.8 um^2.

problems.q: The standard cells of a block have a total area of 319000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 70%. The core has aspect ratio (height over width) 0.5, and the die adds an I/O margin of 13 um on every side of the core. What is the die area, in um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Core area 455714.3 um^2 with H/W = 0.5 gives W = 954.688 um and H = 477.344 um. The die is (W + 26)(H + 26) = 493623.1 um^2.

label: LEF and DEF
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
What a process design kit contains
lesson:
# LEF and DEF

A placer never sees transistors. It reads LEF, which abstracts the technology and each cell into the geometry a placer and router need, and DEF, which records the design: the die, rows, instances and their locations, pins, nets and special wiring. Knowing exactly what each format keeps and drops tells a tool designer what a placement engine can and cannot compute from its inputs.

## What LEF abstracts

LEF (Library Exchange Format) comes in two parts. Technology LEF describes the process for routing: database units, each routing layer with its direction, pitch, width and spacing rules, cut layers and via definitions, and the placement SITE with its width and height. Cell LEF has one MACRO per cell: its class (core, block, pad), size, site, symmetry, every pin with its direction, use (signal, power, ground) and shapes on each layer, and OBS obstructions that block routing over internal metal. What LEF omits matters as much: no transistors, no internal wiring beyond obstructions, no timing, no power. Timing and pin capacitance come from Liberty; full layout comes from GDS. The abstract is small, which is why a placer can load a library of thousands of cells instantly.

## What DEF records

DEF (Design Exchange Format) records one design's physical state. DIEAREA gives the outline. ROW statements give each placement row's site, origin, orientation and site count; TRACKS give routing grids. COMPONENTS lists every instance with its master cell and, once placed, a status (PLACED, FIXED, COVER) with location and orientation. PINS lists the top-level I/O with layers and positions. NETS lists connectivity, and after routing the wire segments; SPECIALNETS holds power and ground rings, stripes and rails. BLOCKAGES and REGIONS restrict placement and routing. Coordinates are integers in database units, declared by UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS, so 2000 means 1 um is 2000 units. A placer reads DEF with COMPONENTS unplaced or roughly placed and writes it back with every standard cell PLACED.

## What a tool can compute from them

From LEF and DEF alone a placer can compute wirelength (from pin positions), density (from cell sizes and rows), legality (rows, sites, orientations, blockages) and a congestion estimate (from track counts and net bounding boxes). It cannot compute timing without Liberty and constraints, and it cannot check manufacturability without full layout and rules. Consistency between formats is an assumption the flow trusts: if a cell's LEF pin shape disagrees with its GDS, the router connects to the wrong place and the error surfaces only at layout-versus-schematic checking. FIXED instances are obstacles the placer must respect, and status flags let a flow freeze macros while re-placing cells. Agents operating a flow should treat these files as the contract between engines.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference (Si2 and Cadence, version 5.8); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), appendix on file formats.

label: DEF units, orientations and pin coordinates
lesson:
# DEF units, orientations and pin coordinates

Every pin coordinate a placer uses comes from combining a cell's LEF pin offset with the instance's DEF location and orientation. Getting this transform wrong silently corrupts wirelength, timing and routing. The arithmetic is simple, but a tool designer must know exactly what the DEF placement point means and how each of the eight orientations maps local coordinates.

## Database units and the placement point

DEF coordinates are integers in database units (DBU). UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 2000 means one micron is 2000 DBU, so PLACED ( 62640 124800 ) puts the instance origin at (31.32, 62.4) um. The placement point is the lower-left corner of the instance's bounding box after the orientation is applied, not the cell's own LEF origin before transformation. A cell of SIZE 2.17 BY 1.6 placed at that point occupies x from 31.32 to 33.49 um and y from 62.4 to 64.0 um in every orientation that keeps its width horizontal. Integers make legality exact: a site grid of 0.19 um at 2000 DBU per um is a step of 380 units, and any location off that grid is illegal.

## Transforming a pin offset

A pin at offset $(p_x, p_y)$ inside a $W \times H$ macro maps as follows. N leaves it at $(p_x, p_y)$. FN mirrors about the vertical axis: $(W - p_x, p_y)$. FS mirrors about the horizontal axis: $(p_x, H - p_y)$. S rotates by 180 degrees: $(W - p_x, H - p_y)$. The rotations by 90 degrees (E, W and their flipped forms) also swap width and height, and standard cells in rows never use them. The absolute pin is the placement point plus the transformed offset. A cell 2.22 by 1.4 um with a pin at (1.46, 1.35), placed FN at (43.32, 30.8), has its pin at $(43.32 + 0.76, 30.8 + 1.35) = (44.08, 32.15)$ um. Note that the mirror subtracts from the macro width, not from the site width or the row height, and that the placement point itself does not move when the orientation changes.

## Why orientation matters to the placer

Rows alternate N and FS so that power rails line up, so legalization must flip a cell when it moves it between an even and an odd row, and every pin position changes when it does. Detailed placers also flip cells deliberately: mirroring a cell to FN can bring its output pin closer to its sink and shorten a net by a fraction of the cell width, a cheap move with no displacement. Wirelength code therefore stores pin offsets per orientation, or transforms on the fly, and incremental updates must recompute a net's bounding box after a flip. Off-by-one errors here, such as forgetting to subtract from $W$ rather than from the site width, produce placements that look legal but have wrong pin locations.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference (version 5.8), sections on COMPONENTS and orientation; the OpenDB documentation in OpenROAD.

problems.q: A LEF macro has SIZE 0.9 BY 2.8 (um) and a pin whose shape is centred at (0.24, 0.12) um in the macro's own coordinates. The DEF file says UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000 and places the instance with PLACED ( 33910 47600 ) N. In DEF the placement point is the lower-left corner of the instance after orientation; FN mirrors about the vertical axis, FS mirrors about the horizontal axis and S rotates by 180 degrees. label: Half-perimeter wirelength
lesson:
# Half-perimeter wirelength

Half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) is the standard estimate of a net's routed length: half the perimeter of the smallest axis-aligned box containing all its pins. Placers minimise it, compare results with it and report it, because it is exact for two- and three-pin nets, a lower bound for all others, and cheap enough to evaluate millions of times per second.

## The bounding box of a net

A net is a hyperedge connecting a set of pins. With pin coordinates $(x_i, y_i)$, its HPWL is
$$\mathrm{HPWL} = \left(\max_i x_i - \min_i x_i\right) + \left(\max_i y_i - \min_i y_i\right).$$
For pins at (2, 7), (10, 3) and (5, 12) the box spans x from 2 to 10 and y from 3 to 12, so HPWL = 8 + 9 = 17. Only the extreme pins matter: moving an interior pin anywhere inside the box leaves HPWL unchanged. The x and y parts are independent, which is why placers often optimise the two dimensions separately. The computation is a single pass over the pins, keeping a running minimum and maximum in each dimension, so it costs time linear in the pin count of the net.

## Total and weighted wirelength

The placement objective is the sum over nets, often weighted: $W = \sum_e w_e \,\mathrm{HPWL}_e$. Weights express priorities: timing-critical nets get larger weights, clock and high-fanout nets may be excluded or down-weighted because they are built later by CTS or buffering. Computing the total is linear in the number of pins. For three nets with HPWL 20, 35 and 12 and weights 1, 3 and 2, the objective is $20 + 105 + 24 = 149$. Because HPWL is computed per net, the total parallelises trivially, which GPU placers exploit.

## How good an estimate it is

For two- and three-pin nets, HPWL equals the length of the rectilinear Steiner minimum tree, the shortest possible rectilinear routing. For more pins it is a lower bound, and the Steiner tree can be noticeably longer for nets with many pins spread across the box; empirical correction factors that grow with pin count are sometimes applied. HPWL also ignores detours caused by congestion and blockages. Its other weakness is mathematical: max and min are not differentiable when two pins tie for the extreme, so gradient-based placers replace it by smooth approximations, while detailed placers use it directly because they evaluate discrete moves.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 4.2 on wirelength estimation.

label: Incremental HPWL after a cell move
lesson:
# Incremental HPWL after a cell move

Detailed placers and annealers evaluate thousands of candidate moves per second, and each one needs the change in wirelength. Recomputing every net is far too slow. Incremental HPWL updates only the nets touching the moved cell, and with careful bookkeeping only the boxes that actually change, which is the difference between a usable and an unusable local optimiser.

## Only incident nets change

When cell $c$ moves from $p$ to $p'$, only the nets that contain one of $c$'s pins can change length. The change in total wirelength is
$$\Delta W = \sum_{e \ni c} w_e\left(\mathrm{HPWL}_e(p') - \mathrm{HPWL}_e(p)\right).$$
A placer stores, for each cell, the list of its nets (the netlist hypergraph's incidence lists), so this sum touches a handful of nets regardless of design size. Example: $c$ moves from (20, 20) to (30, 25) and is on one net with other pins at (10, 15) and (25, 40). The box was 15 by 25 (HPWL 40) and becomes 20 by 25 (HPWL 45), so $\Delta W = 5$.

## Recomputing a box after a move

For each affected net, the new box can often be found without a full rescan. If the cell moves outward, the box simply grows to include the new position. If the cell was the unique extreme pin on some side and moves inward, the box may shrink, and the new extreme must be found among the other pins. Keeping for each net its minimum and maximum together with the count of pins at each extreme makes most updates constant time: the rescan is needed only when the count of pins at an extreme drops to zero. For a three-net example where a cell leaves the left edge of one box, enters the interior of a second and pushes out the top of a third, the three deltas are computed separately and summed.

## Cost and correctness in practice

Incremental evaluation turns a move from $O(\text{pins in the design})$ to $O(\text{pins on the cell's nets})$, which for typical cells is a few dozen. High-fanout nets break this: a cell on a 5000-pin net makes every move expensive, so placers often skip or cap such nets in detailed placement. Two classic bugs are double-counting a net that contains two pins of the moved cell, and evaluating a swap of two cells as two independent moves when they share a net: the shared net must be evaluated with both cells moved. Differential tests against a full recomputation on random moves catch both.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 4 on detailed placement; the OpenROAD dpl source for its incremental cost evaluation.

label: Clique and star net models
prereqs: Clique and star models of a net
lesson:
# Clique and star net models

Quadratic placement works only with two-pin connections, so every multi-pin net must be replaced by a graph of weighted two-pin edges. The clique and star models are the two classic substitutions. Their weights decide how a net pulls on its cells, and their edge counts decide whether the linear system stays sparse enough to solve.

## The clique model

The clique model joins every pair of a $k$-pin net's pins with an edge, $k(k-1)/2$ edges in total. Its quadratic wirelength in x is $w\sum_{i<j}(x_i - x_j)^2$. A common weight is $w = 1/(k-1)$, chosen so that large nets are not overweighted relative to small ones: a $k$-pin clique has many more edges than a two-pin net. For a three-pin net at x = 0, 4 and 10 the pairwise squared distances are 16, 100 and 36, summing to 152, and with weight $1/2$ the cost is 76. Other weightings, such as $2/k$, appear in the literature; the choice is a modeling decision, not a law.

## The star model

The star model adds one auxiliary movable node $s$ per net and connects it to each of the $k$ pins, $k$ edges in total. With unit weights its cost is $\sum_i (x_i - x_s)^2$, minimised when $x_s$ is the mean of the pins. For pins at 0, 4 and 10 the mean is 4.667 and the cost is $21.78 + 0.44 + 28.44 = 50.67$. A useful identity links the two models: $\sum_{i<j}(x_i - x_j)^2 = k\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2$, so with the star node at the mean, a clique of weight $w$ equals a star of weight $kw$. In that sense the two are equivalent, and the star is the sparse one.

## Sparsity and choosing a model

A 100-pin net is 4950 clique edges but only 100 star edges plus one extra variable. Because quadratic placement solves a sparse linear system whose nonzeros are these edges, cliques on large nets would make the matrix dense and the solve slow. Practical placers therefore use cliques for small nets and stars for large ones, with a threshold of a few pins. Both models still share a deeper problem: a quadratic cost grows with the square of distance, so it over-penalises long nets and does not match HPWL. The bound-to-bound model fixes that by choosing edges and weights from the current placement so that the quadratic cost equals HPWL.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 4.3; Viswanathan and Chu, "FastPlace" (ISPD 2004), on hybrid net models.

label: The bound-to-bound net model
lesson:
# The bound-to-bound net model

The bound-to-bound (B2B) net model, introduced with the Kraftwerk2 placer, replaces each net by two-pin edges chosen from the current placement so that the quadratic objective reproduces HPWL exactly at that placement. It combines the fast linear solve of quadratic placement with the accuracy of HPWL, and it underlies modern quadratic placers such as SimPL.

## Edges between the bounds

Sort a net's pins by x. The two extreme pins are the bounds. B2B connects the bounds to each other and connects every inner pin to both bounds; inner pins are not connected to each other. A $k$-pin net gets $1 + 2(k-2) = 2k - 3$ edges, linear in $k$ like the star model, with no extra variables. The y dimension is modeled separately, with its own bounds, so a pin can be a bound in x and an inner pin in y. For pins at x = 3, 8, 15 and 21 the bounds are 3 and 21, and the edges are 3-21, 8-3, 8-21, 15-3 and 15-21.

## Weights that reproduce HPWL

Each edge gets weight $w_{ij} = \frac{1}{(k-1)\,|x_i - x_j|}$, computed from the current positions. Then each edge contributes $w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2 = |x_i - x_j|/(k-1)$. The bound edge contributes $L/(k-1)$, where $L$ is the net's span, and every inner pin contributes its distances to both bounds, which add to $L$. The total is $(L + (k-2)L)/(k-1) = L$: the quadratic cost equals the x span exactly. Some papers write the weight as $2/((k-1)|x_i - x_j|)$, which only scales the objective. In the example above, $L = 18$ and the edge 8-3 has weight $1/(3 \cdot 5) = 0.0667$. The weights are large for short edges and small for long ones, which is exactly what converts a squared distance back into a linear one.

## Iterating the model

Once the weights are fixed, the quadratic system is solved and cells move, so the bounds and distances change and the model is no longer exact. B2B placers therefore iterate: build the model from the current placement, solve, rebuild, solve again, converging toward a placement that minimises HPWL subject to the spreading forces. Two practical details matter. Pins that coincide make $|x_i - x_j| = 0$, so implementations clamp the distance to a small minimum to avoid infinite weights. And because the edges change every iteration, the matrix structure changes too, so the solver reassembles it; conjugate gradient with a warm start from the previous solution keeps each solve cheap.

## Going deeper

Spindler, Schlichtmann and Johannes, "Kraftwerk2, a fast force-directed quadratic placement approach using an accurate net model" (IEEE TCAD, 2008); Kim, Lee and Markov, "SimPL: an effective placement algorithm" (ICCAD 2010).

label: Steiner and spanning-tree wirelength estimates
prereqs: Minimum spanning trees for net estimation
lesson:
# Steiner and spanning-tree wirelength estimates

A routed net is a rectilinear tree, and its shortest form is the rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT). Placers usually optimise HPWL, a lower bound, but timing estimation, congestion models and final reporting need a tree length. Spanning trees and Steiner trees bracket the truth, and knowing when each is exact tells a tool designer which estimate to use where.

## Three pins: HPWL is exact

For a three-pin net, the RSMT connects the pins through a single Steiner point at (median x, median y), and its length equals the HPWL. Pins at (0, 0), (10, 4) and (6, 12) have median point (6, 4); the three branches have lengths 10, 4 and 8, total 22, while the bounding box is 10 by 12, HPWL 22. Two-pin nets are trivially exact as well. Since most nets in real designs have two or three pins, HPWL is an exact routed-length estimate for the majority of nets, ignoring detours. The gap opens only for larger nets.

## Spanning trees as an upper estimate

A rectilinear minimum spanning tree (RMST) connects pins only to each other with Manhattan edges. Prim's algorithm builds it in $O(n^2)$ for $n$ pins, or $O(n \log n)$ with geometric tricks. Hwang's theorem bounds its quality: the RMST is at most $3/2$ times the RSMT. For pins at (0, 0), (10, 0), (0, 10) and (10, 10), the RMST uses three edges of length 10, total 30, while the HPWL is 20. The RMST is easy and gives a valid routing topology, which is why it is used as a starting point for Steiner heuristics and for Elmore-delay estimation of nets.

## Steiner points on the Hanan grid

Hanan's theorem says some RSMT has all its Steiner points on the Hanan grid, the intersections of the horizontal and vertical lines through the pins, and at most $n - 2$ Steiner points are ever needed. That turns the search into a finite one. Take four pins at (0, 5), (5, 0), (10, 5) and (5, 10). Their Hanan grid has lines at x = 0, 5, 10 and y = 0, 5, 10, so (5, 5) is a candidate. A star from (5, 5) has four arms of length 5, total 20, equal to the HPWL; the best spanning tree needs three edges of length 10, total 30. This instance meets Hwang's 3/2 bound exactly. Exact RSMT is NP-hard in general, so tools use fast methods such as the FLUTE lookup tables, which are optimal for small nets (up to nine pins) and heuristic beyond.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), sections 4.2 and 5.6; Chu and Wong, "FLUTE: fast lookup table based rectilinear Steiner minimal tree algorithm" (IEEE TCAD, 2008).

label: Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio
prereqs: Core utilization, aspect ratio and die size
lesson:
# Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio

A floorplan arranges blocks, such as macros, hard IP or soft partitions, inside an outline. Its first measurable qualities are the area it uses, the whitespace it wastes and its shape. Every floorplanning algorithm, from annealing over Polish expressions to fixed-outline sequence-pair packers, scores candidates with these numbers before any wirelength term is added.

## Outline area and whitespace

The floorplan's area is the area of the bounding box of all blocks, or the given outline in a fixed-outline flow. Whitespace, also called dead space, is the outline area not covered by blocks:
$$\text{whitespace} = \frac{A_{outline} - \sum_b A_b}{A_{outline}}.$$
Three blocks of areas 200, 130 and 442 um$^2$ in a 38 by 24 um outline (912 um$^2$) leave 140 um$^2$, which is 15.4% whitespace. Some whitespace is wanted: it becomes routing channels, room for buffers and space for the standard cells that surround hard macros. But whitespace that comes from a poor arrangement is simply wasted die area, and the floorplanner tries to minimise it subject to the other goals.

## Packing and its bounding box

When blocks are packed by a representation, the outline is their bounding box, so whitespace depends on how the shapes fit. Two blocks of 49 by 37 and 24 by 28 placed side by side, bottoms aligned, have a bounding box 73 wide and 37 tall, 2701 um$^2$, of which the blocks cover 2485 um$^2$: 8.0% whitespace, all of it above the shorter block. Stacking the same blocks instead gives a 49 by 65 box, 3185 um$^2$ and 22.0% whitespace. Mismatched heights in a row or mismatched widths in a column are the main source of waste, which is why floorplanners consider block rotation and, for soft blocks, variable aspect ratios.

## Fixed outlines and aspect ratio

Classical floorplanning minimises area freely, but in a hierarchical design the block's outline is dictated by the parent floorplan, so modern floorplanners solve a fixed-outline problem: fit all blocks inside a given W by H with a maximum whitespace. Given total block area $A$, a fixed height $H$ and allowed whitespace fraction $\gamma$, the outline width must be at least $A/((1-\gamma)H)$. For 9000 um$^2$ of blocks, height 91 um and 5% whitespace, the width is $9000/(0.95 \cdot 91) = 104.11$ um. The aspect ratio $H/W$ is then a constraint rather than an outcome, and annealers add a penalty for exceeding the outline. Fixed-outline packing is markedly harder than free packing, because many candidate packings that are compact are still the wrong shape.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 3; Adya and Markov, "Fixed-outline floorplanning: enabling hierarchical design" (IEEE TVLSI, 2003).

label: Slicing floorplans
prereqs: Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio
Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Slicing floorplans

A slicing floorplan is one that can be produced by repeatedly cutting a rectangle into two with a straight horizontal or vertical line. Its structure is a binary tree whose leaves are blocks and whose internal nodes are cuts, which makes area evaluation a single bottom-up pass and orientation optimisation polynomial. That convenience is why slicing structures were the first practical floorplan representation.

## Cuts and the slicing tree

Start with the chip rectangle and cut it with a vertical line into a left and right part, or with a horizontal line into a bottom and top part, then cut each part again, until each piece holds one block. The record of cuts is a slicing tree: each internal node is a V (vertical) or H (horizontal) cut, its children are the two sub-floorplans, and the leaves are blocks. A vertical cut puts children side by side; a horizontal cut stacks them. Not every floorplan is slicing: the smallest non-slicing arrangement is the wheel, or pinwheel, of five blocks spiralling around a centre, where no straight line crosses the whole chip without cutting a block.

## Evaluating the area bottom-up

For fixed block shapes, each node's dimensions follow from its children's. A vertical cut adds widths and takes the larger height: $(w_l + w_r, \max(h_l, h_r))$. A horizontal cut takes the larger width and adds heights: $(\max(w_l, w_r), h_l + h_r)$. A post-order traversal computes the root's dimensions in time linear in the number of blocks. Example: blocks A (5 by 6), B (3 by 9), C (3 by 10). Node r2 is a vertical cut of B and A: $(8, 9)$. The root is a horizontal cut with C below and r2 above: $(\max(3, 8), 10 + 9) = (8, 19)$, area 152. The blocks cover 87, so 65 um$^2$ is whitespace.

## Why slicing structures are useful and limited

Slicing trees make several hard problems easy. Area evaluation is linear time. Choosing the best orientation or shape of every block, given each block's candidate shapes, is polynomial for slicing floorplans (Stockmeyer's algorithm, by combining shape curves bottom-up), while it is NP-hard for general floorplans. Incremental evaluation after a local change only recomputes the path to the root. The cost is expressiveness: some optimal packings are non-slicing, and forcing a slicing structure can waste area, especially with many differently shaped blocks. Slicing structures also map naturally onto hierarchical channel routing, which is part of why they persisted.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 3.4; Stockmeyer, "Optimal orientations of cells in slicing floorplan designs" (Information and Control, 1983).

label: Normalized Polish expressions
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Normalized Polish expressions

A Polish expression is the post-order traversal of a slicing tree, written as a string of block names and cut operators. Wong and Liu showed that normalized Polish expressions correspond one-to-one with slicing floorplans, giving simulated annealing a compact, unambiguous search space with cheap moves. Evaluating one is a stack computation that every floorplanner of this family runs millions of times.

## From tree to postfix string

Write a slicing tree in post-order: left subtree, right subtree, then the operator. Operands are blocks; operators are V (side by side, left operand on the left) and H (stacked, left operand below). The tree with root H, left child block 1 and right child a V cut of blocks 2 and 3 becomes 1 2 3 V H. Every valid expression has the balloting property: reading left to right, every prefix contains more operands than operators, and the whole string has $n$ operands and $n - 1$ operators. A slicing floorplan can have several trees, because a run of the same cut can be grouped in different ways, so several expressions can describe one floorplan.

## Evaluating with a stack

Read the expression left to right. Push each block's shape. On an operator, pop the right operand, then the left, combine them (V adds widths and takes the larger height; H takes the larger width and adds heights) and push the result. The last shape on the stack is the floorplan. For 1 2 3 V H with blocks 1 = 7 by 6, 2 = 7 by 2 and 3 = 10 by 9: push 1, 2 and 3; V pops 3 and 2 and pushes (17, 9); H pops (17, 9) and 1 and pushes $(\max(7, 17), 6 + 9) = (17, 15)$. The area is 255, and with 146 um$^2$ of blocks, 109 um$^2$ is whitespace. The cost is linear in the expression length.

## Normalization makes the encoding unique

A Polish expression is normalized if it has no two identical operators in a row, such as V V or H H. Normalized expressions correspond to skewed slicing trees, where no node has a right child with the same operator, and Wong and Liu proved that each slicing floorplan has exactly one normalized expression. That removes redundancy from the search space: an annealer exploring normalized expressions never wastes moves on different strings for the same floorplan. The moves M1, M2 and M3 are designed to keep expressions normalized and balloting, or to be checked and rejected when they would not. The number of distinct slicing structures still grows exponentially with $n$, so search rather than enumeration is required.

## Going deeper

Wong and Liu, "A new algorithm for floorplan design" (DAC 1986); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 3.5.

label: The M1, M2 and M3 moves
lesson:
# The M1, M2 and M3 moves

Simulated annealing over normalized Polish expressions needs a move set that can reach every slicing floorplan, changes the floorplan a little at a time and keeps expressions valid. Wong and Liu's three moves, M1, M2 and M3, do exactly that. Implementing them correctly, including the legality check M3 needs, is a standard exercise in designing a search space for a combinatorial optimiser.

## M1: swap adjacent operands

M1 picks two operands that are adjacent in the sequence of operands, ignoring operators between them, and swaps them. In 6 3 H 2 4 V 5 1 H V H, operands 4 and 5 are adjacent in the operand order 6, 3, 2, 4, 5, 1, so M1 gives 6 3 H 2 5 V 4 1 H V H. Every operator stays where it was, so the tree shape is unchanged and only two leaves trade places; balloting and normalization are automatically preserved. The effect on the floorplan is two blocks exchanging positions, which changes area when their shapes differ and wirelength when their connections differ.

## M2: complement a chain

A chain is a maximal run of consecutive operators, such as V H V. M2 picks one chain and complements every operator in it, turning V into H and H into V. In 1 4 V 3 V 2 5 H V the chains are V, V and H V; complementing the second gives 1 4 V 3 H 2 5 H V. Because a normalized chain alternates, its complement alternates too, so the result is normalized; operand and operator counts do not change, so balloting holds. Geometrically, M2 turns side-by-side arrangements into stacked ones at several levels of the tree at once, a larger move than M1. Complementing only part of a chain could create two equal adjacent operators, which is why the whole chain flips.

## M3: swap an operand and an operator, with a check

M3 swaps an adjacent operand and operator, which changes the tree's shape and is the only move that lets the search reach different tree topologies. It can break validity in two ways. Moving an operator left can violate balloting, leaving a prefix with as many operators as operands, as in 1 H 4 2 3 H 5 H V, which starts with an operator after one operand. It can also create two identical adjacent operators, as in 1 4 H 2 3 H H 5 V. The annealer therefore checks the candidate: count operands and operators along the prefix and compare neighbours, both linear time, and the check can be made constant time by tracking counts at the swap position. Rejected candidates are simply redrawn. Together the three moves connect the whole space of normalized expressions.

## Going deeper

Wong and Liu, "A new algorithm for floorplan design" (DAC 1986); Sarrafzadeh and Wong, "An Introduction to VLSI Physical Design" (1996), chapter on floorplanning.

label: Shape functions and block orientation
lesson:
# Shape functions and block orientation

Blocks often have more than one allowed shape: a hard macro may rotate, and a soft block may take any aspect ratio within limits. A shape function lists a block's achievable (width, height) pairs. Combining shape functions up a slicing tree, keeping only the non-dominated pairs, finds the best orientation of every block at once, which is Stockmeyer's classical result for slicing floorplans.

## Shapes of one block

A shape function of a block is the set of (width, height) pairs it can take. A rotatable hard block of 8 by 15 has two: (8, 15) and (15, 8). A soft block of area 120 with aspect ratio between 0.5 and 2 has a continuous curve $h = 120/w$ for $w$ between about 7.75 and 15.5. A pair is dominated if another pair is no wider and no taller, since the dominated shape can never help. The remaining non-dominated pairs form a staircase: as width grows, height falls. Listing a hard block's shapes is trivial, but this staircase view is what makes combination efficient.

## Combining two blocks under a cut

Under a vertical cut, each choice of shapes $(w_a, h_a)$ and $(w_b, h_b)$ gives a combined shape $(w_a + w_b, \max(h_a, h_b))$; under a horizontal cut, $(\max(w_a, w_b), h_a + h_b)$. With A = 8 by 15 rotatable and B = 11 by 10 fixed, a vertical cut gives (19, 15) or (26, 10), areas 285 and 260, so rotating A wins. With both blocks rotatable there are four combinations. Pruning dominated results after each combination keeps the list short: for staircases of sizes $m$ and $n$ the non-dominated combined list has at most $m + n - 1$ entries and can be built by a merge-like walk, not by trying all $mn$ pairs.

## Orientation optimisation on a slicing tree

Stockmeyer's algorithm computes the shape function of every node bottom-up, pruning dominated pairs, and picks the smallest-area shape at the root; a top-down pass then recovers each block's chosen orientation. For slicing floorplans this is polynomial, roughly linear in the number of blocks times the length of the shape lists. For general non-slicing floorplans the same orientation problem is NP-hard, which is one reason slicing representations remained popular. Fixed-outline floorplanners use the root's shape function differently: instead of minimum area they pick the shape that fits the outline, or report that none does. In an annealer, the shape computation runs inside every move evaluation, so its cost directly limits the number of moves per second.

## Going deeper

Stockmeyer, "Optimal orientations of cells in slicing floorplan designs" (Information and Control, 1983); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 3.6.

label: Sequence pairs
prereqs: Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio
lesson:
# Sequence pairs

A sequence pair encodes any packing of rectangles, slicing or not, as two permutations of the block names. Introduced by Murata and colleagues in the mid-1990s, it turns the geometric relations between blocks into two constraint graphs whose longest paths give the coordinates. It is the standard non-slicing representation for annealing-based and fixed-outline floorplanners.

## Reading relations from two sequences

A sequence pair is $(\Gamma_+, \Gamma_-)$, two orderings of the $n$ blocks. For two blocks a and b: if a precedes b in both sequences, a is left of b; if a follows b in $\Gamma_+$ but precedes it in $\Gamma_-$, a is below b. Every pair of blocks gets exactly one of these relations (or the mirrored ones), so the pair fully specifies a topology. With $\Gamma_+ = (A\ C\ D\ B\ E)$ and $\Gamma_- = (A\ B\ E\ D\ C)$: A precedes everything in both, so A is left of all; B and E keep order in both, so B is left of E; D precedes B in $\Gamma_+$ but follows it in $\Gamma_-$, so B is below D. There are $(n!)^2$ sequence pairs.

## Packing by longest paths

The left-of relations form a horizontal constraint graph: an edge from a to b with length $w_a$ whenever a is left of b. Each block's x coordinate is the longest path to it from a source at x = 0, and the chip width is the longest path overall. The below relations form a vertical graph with edge lengths $h_a$, giving y coordinates and height. Both graphs are acyclic, and processing blocks in $\Gamma_-$ order is a valid topological order for both, so a simple $O(n^2)$ double loop computes the packing. In the example with A = 6 by 3, B = 8 by 7, C = 7 by 3, D = 2 by 2 and E = 4 by 1, the x coordinates are 0, 6, 6, 6 and 14 and the chip is 18 wide.

## Annealing over sequence pairs

Annealers perturb a sequence pair by swapping two blocks in one sequence, swapping them in both, or rotating a block, then re-pack and evaluate. Any packing can be represented, so the search is complete, but the space has redundancy: many sequence pairs give the same packing. Evaluation cost is the bottleneck. The $O(n^2)$ longest-path packing can be replaced by $O(n \log n)$ methods based on weighted longest common subsequences (the FAST-SP approach), which matters when an annealer evaluates millions of moves. For fixed-outline problems, the cost function adds penalties for width and height beyond the outline, and wirelength is computed from block centres or pin offsets after packing.

## Going deeper

Murata, Fujiyoshi, Nakatake and Kajitani, "VLSI module placement based on rectangle-packing by the sequence-pair" (IEEE TCAD, 1996); Tang, Tian and Wong, "FAST-SP: a fast algorithm for block placement based on sequence pair" (ASP-DAC 2001).

label: B*-trees and contour packing
prereqs: Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio
Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# B*-trees and contour packing

A B*-tree encodes a compacted floorplan as an ordered binary tree: left children sit to the right of their parent, right children sit above it at the same x. Packing is a single pre-order traversal with a contour that tracks the skyline of placed blocks. Its linear-time packing and simple moves made it a popular representation for annealing floorplanners and for analog placement with symmetry constraints.

## Left children right, right children up

The root block sits at the origin. For a node b with parent p: if b is p's left child, b is placed immediately to the right of p, at $x_b = x_p + w_p$; if b is p's right child, b is placed above p at the same x, $x_b = x_p$. So the x coordinates follow directly from the tree: walk from the root and add the parent's width on each left edge. With A = 2 by 4 at the root, B as A's left child (x = 2), D as B's left child (x = 2 + 5 = 7), and C as B's right child (x = 2), every block's x is known before any y is computed. The tree represents admissible placements, those compacted to the left and bottom.

## Dropping blocks onto a contour

The y coordinate is found by dropping the block from above onto what is already placed: $y_b$ is the highest top edge among placed blocks that overlap b's x interval. Blocks are placed in pre-order (node, left subtree, right subtree), which guarantees that the blocks a node can rest on have already been placed. A contour data structure, a doubly linked list of horizontal segments describing the current skyline, answers each query and is updated by splicing in the new block's top edge. With amortised constant work per block, the whole packing is $O(n)$. Example: A = 8 by 2 at the origin, its left child B = 2 by 5 at x = 8, and its right child C = 4 by 1 at x = 0, which lands on A at y = 2.

## Moves and uses

Annealing over B*-trees uses three moves: rotate a block, move a node to another position in the tree, and swap two nodes. Each move changes only part of the packing, though a fresh pre-order pass is simple and linear. Compared with sequence pairs, B*-trees represent only admissible placements, compacted left and down, which loses nothing for area minimisation; compared with Polish expressions, they also represent non-slicing floorplans. Extensions handle symmetry groups for analog layout, where mirrored device pairs must share an axis, and fixed-outline constraints. Because packing is cheap, B*-tree annealers can run millions of moves on designs with tens to hundreds of blocks.

## Going deeper

Chang, Chang, Wu and Wu, "B*-trees: a new representation for non-slicing floorplans" (DAC 2000); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 3.

label: Floorplanning by simulated annealing
prereqs: The M1, M2 and M3 moves
lesson:
# Floorplanning by simulated annealing

Simulated annealing is the classic search engine for floorplanning: propose a move on the representation, evaluate the new floorplan's cost, accept improvements always and worsenings with a probability that falls as the temperature cools. Its quality depends on the cost function, the move set and the cooling schedule, all of which a floorplanner designer chooses and tunes.

## A cost that mixes area and wirelength

A typical floorplan cost is $C = \alpha A + \beta W$, the bounding-box area plus the total wirelength between blocks, with terms for outline violation, aspect ratio or timing as needed. The weights balance quantities with different units, so they are usually normalised by the values of a reference floorplan. Each move is evaluated by the change $\Delta C = C_{new} - C_{old}$. With $C = A + 2W$, a move from A = 526, W = 499 to A = 470, W = 435 changes the cost from 1524 to 1340, $\Delta C = -184$, a clear improvement. Wirelength between blocks is estimated by HPWL over block centres or pin positions after packing.

## The Metropolis acceptance rule

An improving move ($\Delta C \le 0$) is always accepted. A worsening move is accepted with probability $e^{-\Delta C/T}$. At T = 80 a move that raises cost by 56 is accepted with probability $e^{-0.7} = 0.4966$; at T = 10 the same move is accepted with probability $e^{-5.6} = 0.0037$. Early, at high temperature, the search wanders freely and escapes poor local minima; late, at low temperature, it behaves like greedy descent. A random number drawn uniformly in [0, 1) is compared against the probability. The rule is the same for Polish expressions, sequence pairs and B*-trees: only the move set and packing change.

## The cooling schedule

The temperature starts high enough that most uphill moves are accepted and is lowered by a schedule, most simply geometric: $T_{k+1} = r T_k$ with $r$ around 0.85 to 0.95, holding each temperature for a number of moves proportional to the problem size. The number of temperature steps from $T_0$ to $T_f$ is the smallest $k$ with $T_0 r^k < T_f$, that is $k > \ln(T_f/T_0)/\ln r$: from 2000 to below 0.5 at $r = 0.9$ takes 79 steps. Slower cooling gives better results and longer runs. Fixed-outline floorplanners such as Parquet add outline-violation penalties and moves aimed at pulling the packing into the outline. Annealing is easy to implement and to extend with new cost terms, which is why it remains common for macro-scale problems.

## Going deeper

Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi, "Optimization by simulated annealing" (Science, 1983); Adya and Markov, "Fixed-outline floorplanning: enabling hierarchical design" (IEEE TVLSI, 2003), on the Parquet floorplanner.

label: Macro placement
prereqs: Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio
lesson:
# Macro placement

Macros (memories, register files, analog and IP blocks) are tens to thousands of times larger than standard cells, and their positions shape everything else: where connected logic can go, where routing channels form and how the power grid reaches them. Macro placement is usually done during floorplanning, by engineers, scripts or dedicated placers, and then frozen before standard-cell placement.

## What a good macro placement looks like

Good macro placements share a few traits. Macros sit near the core boundary or are clustered, leaving a large contiguous region for standard cells, rather than scattered across the middle where they would fragment rows and force detours. Pins face the logic they connect to. Macros that exchange wide buses sit close together, following the design's dataflow. Each macro carries a halo, a keep-out margin where no standard cell may sit, which leaves room for pin access and power connections. Narrow channels between macros are avoided, or blocked for placement, because cells placed there are hard to route to. Orientation matters as much as position: flipping a memory can turn its pin edge from the die boundary toward the core.

## Sizing the channel between macros

When macros must face each other, the channel between them must carry the nets that cross it. With $N$ nets crossing, $L$ routing layers in the crossing direction and track pitch $p$, the channel needs at least $\lceil N/L \rceil$ tracks, or $\lceil N/L \rceil p$ of width, plus a halo $h$ on each side: width $\ge \lceil N/L \rceil p + 2h$. For 220 nets, 3 layers, a 0.4 um pitch and 10 um halos, that is $74 \times 0.4 + 20 = 49.6$ um. Real estimates add margin for power stripes, blockages and imperfect track use. A channel that is too narrow shows up later as routing overflow, which the router cannot fix without moving the macros.

## How macro placement is automated and judged

Automated macro placers include annealing over block representations, analytical mixed-size placement that places macros and cells together and then legalizes and fixes the macros, and learning-based approaches. Whatever the method, macro placement is optimised through a cheap proxy (wirelength, density and congestion estimates), and its real quality appears only after standard cells are placed and routed. A placement with a good proxy score can still be congested if the proxy misses routing demand. Flows therefore evaluate candidate macro placements by running the rest of placement, at least approximately, and comparing final metrics. OpenROAD provides macro placement through engines such as its RTL-MP hierarchical macro placer, operating on the same database as global placement.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 3; the OpenROAD documentation for macro placement.

label: Pin and I/O assignment
lesson:
# Pin and I/O assignment

Pins on a block's boundary, whether chip I/O or the ports of a hierarchical partition, must be assigned to legal slots. Their locations pull the connected logic toward them, so a bad assignment lengthens every net that leaves the block. Pin assignment is a matching problem, solved exactly by the Hungarian algorithm or approximately by fast heuristics inside floorplanning loops.

## Pins, slots and costs

A block boundary offers legal slots: positions on allowed layers at the right pitch, outside blockages. Each pin connects to logic inside, or to the outside world, at some location. The cost of putting pin $i$ in slot $j$ is an estimate of the wirelength this creates, most simply the Manhattan distance from the slot to the pin's connected cell or to the centroid of its connected cells. For a 100 by 100 um block with pin p1 connecting to a cell at (57, 29) and a slot at (37, 0), the cost is $20 + 29 = 49$. The assignment's total cost is the sum over pins. Additional constraints include pin groups that must stay together, spacing, and pins restricted to one side.

## Optimal assignment as matching

Assigning $n$ pins to $n$ slots with one pin per slot and minimum total cost is the linear assignment problem, a minimum-cost perfect matching in a bipartite graph. The Hungarian algorithm solves it in $O(n^3)$; for a handful of pins, checking all $n!$ permutations works too. With more slots than pins, dummy pins with zero cost make the problem square. For three pins there are six assignments, and evaluating each and keeping the cheapest gives the optimum. The improvement over a naive assignment, such as pins in netlist order around the boundary, can be large because a single badly placed pin drags its logic across the block.

## Pin assignment in the flow

Pin assignment and placement depend on each other: pins should go near their logic, but the logic is placed near its pins. Flows break the cycle by iterating: place with initial pins, reassign pins to the placed logic, then place again. For chip-level I/O, constraints from the package and the board often fix the order, leaving only fine adjustment. For hierarchical blocks, pins on both sides of a boundary must agree, so assignment is done at the parent level. OpenROAD's ioPlacer assigns pins with a matching formulation over slots on the die boundary and supports constraints such as allowed edges and pin groups. Because it is fast, an agent can rerun it after any floorplan change.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 3.7 on pin assignment; the OpenROAD documentation for ioPlacer.

label: Power planning: rings, stripes and rails
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# Power planning: rings, stripes and rails

Every cell needs VDD and VSS, so the floorplan includes a power distribution network: rings around the core and macros, stripes on upper metal layers across the core, and rails along every standard-cell row. Its geometry consumes routing resource and limits where cells and wires can go, so the placer must know it, and its density sets the IR drop the design will see.

## Rings, stripes and rails

A power grid starts with rings of VDD and VSS around the core and often around each macro. Stripes, also called straps, run across the core on upper layers, in pairs of VDD and VSS at a regular pitch, alternating direction on successive layers to form a mesh. At the bottom, each row has rails on metal 1 along its top and bottom edges, which the cells touch by abutment; vias connect rails to the stripes above. The stripes are placed from an offset at a fixed pitch: a 1040 um core with a first stripe pair at 19 um and a 25 um pitch gets $\lfloor (1040 - 19)/25 \rfloor + 1 = 41$ pairs. OpenROAD's pdngen builds such grids from a specification of layers, widths, pitches and offsets.

## The routing cost of the grid

Power wiring occupies tracks that signal routing cannot use. If every 20 um of a layer carries a VDD and a VSS stripe each 1.5 um wide, 3 um of every 20 um, 15%, is gone. Dense grids reduce IR drop and electromigration risk but steal routing capacity, especially on the layers that carry long signal wires. Stripes also cut the space available near macros and may block pin access if placed carelessly, which is why power planning follows macro placement. The placer sees the grid as routing blockage in congestion estimates, and sometimes as placement blockage where vias stacks land on cell pins, so a placer that ignores it will underestimate congestion.

## IR drop along a rail

A row's rail is a resistor carrying current to the cells along it. With the rail fed at both ends by stripes, total current $I$ drawn uniformly along its length and rail resistance $R$ between the stripes, the voltage drop is largest at the midpoint, where it equals $IR/8$. A 110 um rail at 0.1 ohm/um has $R = 11$ ohm, and 5 mA gives $5 \times 11/8 = 6.875$ mV. Because $R$ grows with stripe pitch and the current fed by one segment also grows with pitch, the drop grows with the square of the pitch: halving the pitch quarters it. That quadratic law is how a planner sizes stripe pitch for a drop budget, before a full IR analysis confirms it. Dense logic placed in one region raises local current, so placement and power planning interact.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 3.8 on power and ground routing; the OpenROAD documentation for pdngen.

label: The global placement problem
prereqs: Core utilization, aspect ratio and die size
lesson:
# The global placement problem

Global placement decides roughly where every standard cell goes. Stated exactly it is a huge, NP-hard, discrete problem; every practical placer solves a relaxation of it. Knowing the decision variables, the objective, the density constraint and the relaxations each placer family makes is the map a tool designer needs before reading any particular algorithm.

## Variables, objective and constraint

The decision variables are the coordinates $(x_i, y_i)$ of every movable cell; macros and I/O pins are usually fixed. The objective is total weighted wirelength, $\sum_e w_e \,\mathrm{WL}_e(x, y)$, with HPWL as the usual measure. The constraint is density: for every bin $b$ of a grid over the placement region, the movable cell area inside it must not exceed a target fraction $\rho_t$ of the bin's free area. Without the constraint, minimising wirelength collapses connected cells onto one point. Legality (rows, sites, no overlap) is not imposed here; it is deferred to legalization. A target density below 1, for example 0.7, also leaves room for later buffering and routing.

## Three families of relaxation

Min-cut placers relax geometry into partitioning: recursively bisect the netlist and the region, minimising nets cut at each level. Quadratic placers replace wirelength by a sum of squared two-pin distances, whose minimum solves a sparse linear system, and handle density by separate spreading steps. Nonlinear analytical placers smooth HPWL with log-sum-exp or weighted-average functions and add a differentiable density penalty, $\min_x W(x) + \lambda D(x)$, solved by gradient methods. Electrostatics-based placers such as ePlace, RePlAce and DREAMPlace belong to the last family, with density modeled as electric potential energy. Each family trades accuracy of the wirelength model, quality of the spreading model and speed.

## Stopping and handing off

Global placement ends before density is perfectly satisfied. Placers track overflow, the fraction of cell area that sits above target in over-full bins, and stop around a small value such as 0.1, because squeezing out the last overflow costs wirelength that legalization can recover more cheaply with small moves. The handoff has failure modes. A low average overflow can hide local hot spots that force long legalization moves. Fixed pins and macros are essential: in quadratic placement they anchor the linear system, and without them it is singular. And because the objective is wirelength, timing and routability enter only through net weights, density targets and inflation, which must be designed in, not hoped for.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 4; Markov, Hu and Kim, "Progress and challenges in VLSI placement research" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 2015).

label: Min-cut placement
prereqs: The cut size of a partition
lesson:
# Min-cut placement

Min-cut placement was the first scalable approach: cut the region in two, partition the netlist into two halves that minimise the nets crossing, assign each half to a side and recurse. It reuses decades of partitioning algorithms (Kernighan-Lin, Fiduccia-Mattheyses, multilevel hMetis) and, in placers such as Capo, stayed competitive well into the 2000s.

## Bisecting the netlist and the region

At each level, a region and its cells are split by a cut line into two subregions, and the cells are partitioned into two sets with areas matching the subregions' capacities, within a balance tolerance. The partitioner minimises the cut, the number (or weight) of nets with cells on both sides, since every cut net must cross the line and will be long. For cells c3 and c5 on the left and c1, c2, c4, c6 on the right, a net {c3, c4, c6} is cut and a net {c1, c2} is not. Fiduccia-Mattheyses moves cells one at a time by gain, in linear time per pass, and multilevel partitioners coarsen the netlist, partition the small version and refine while uncoarsening.

## Levels of recursion

Each level doubles the number of regions. If every bisection splits cells evenly, after $L$ levels each region holds $n/2^L$ cells, so reaching at most $k$ cells per region takes the smallest $L$ with $n/2^L \le k$, that is $L = \lceil \log_2(n/k) \rceil$. A million cells down to regions of 10 cells takes $\lceil \log_2 10^5 \rceil = 17$ levels. Cut directions usually alternate, vertical then horizontal, or follow the region's aspect ratio so that regions stay roughly square. At the bottom, small regions are placed by enumeration or a simple end-case placer. With linear-time partitioning per level, the whole placement is $O(n \log n)$.

## Terminal propagation

Partitioning a region in isolation ignores the cells outside it. If a cell in the region connects to a cell already placed far to the right, it should go to the right half. Terminal propagation, due to Dunlop and Kernighan, fixes this: each external connection is replaced by a fixed terminal on the side of the cut nearer to it, and the partitioner treats it as a cell locked to that side. A net is cut if its members, including propagated terminals, end up on both sides. For a cell c with nets to a right-propagated terminal, to a left terminal and a left cell, and to three right cells, placing c on the right cuts the nets that also touch the left. Without propagation, min-cut placers produce long nets between regions; with it they track the global structure.

## Going deeper

Dunlop and Kernighan, "A procedure for placement of standard-cell VLSI circuits" (IEEE TCAD, 1985); Caldwell, Kahng and Markov, "Can recursive bisection alone produce routable placements?" (DAC 2000), on the Capo placer.

label: Quadratic placement
lesson:
# Quadratic placement

Quadratic placement replaces each net by two-pin springs and minimises the sum of squared spring lengths. Because the objective is a convex quadratic, its minimum satisfies a linear system that can be solved in near-linear time. GORDIAN, FastPlace, Kraftwerk2 and SimPL are all built on this core, with different net models and spreading methods.

## One movable cell

With two-pin connections of weight $w_j$ from a movable cell to fixed pins at $x_j$, the cost in x is $\sum_j w_j(x - x_j)^2$. Setting the derivative $2\sum_j w_j(x - x_j)$ to zero gives the weighted mean:
$$x^* = \frac{\sum_j w_j x_j}{\sum_j w_j}.$$
For pins at 74 (weight 1) and 1 (weight 3), $x^* = (74 + 3)/4 = 19.25$. The x and y problems separate, so $y^*$ is the weighted mean of the y coordinates. Every cell in a quadratic placement ends up at the weighted mean of everything it connects to, which is both its strength (a closed form) and its weakness (cells pile up in the middle).

## Two or three movable cells

With several movable cells, each cell's optimality condition involves its neighbours. For movable a and b connected with weight 1, a also tied to a fixed pin at 46 and b to one at 45 (weight 1 each), the conditions are $2x_a - x_b = 46$ and $-x_a + 2x_b = 45$, so $x_a = 45.67$ and $x_b = 45.33$. For a chain of three cells, the system is tridiagonal and can be solved by elimination in linear time. In general the conditions form $Ax = b$, where A collects connection weights and b collects weighted fixed-pin coordinates. Solving this system is the whole of one quadratic placement iteration.

## Why quadratic placement needs help

The quadratic solution minimises squared lengths, not HPWL, so it over-penalises long connections and pulls cells inward; the B2B net model corrects the mismatch by re-weighting edges. More seriously, the solution ignores density: highly connected cells cluster near the centre with massive overlap. Quadratic placers therefore alternate the solve with spreading. GORDIAN used partitioning-based constraints; FastPlace used cell shifting; Kraftwerk added density-derived forces; SimPL computes a spread-out target with look-ahead legalization and pulls cells toward it with anchor pseudo-nets. The solve stays cheap because A is sparse, symmetric and positive definite, so preconditioned conjugate gradient handles millions of cells.

## Going deeper

Kleinhans, Sigl, Johannes and Antreich, "GORDIAN: VLSI placement by quadratic programming and slicing optimization" (IEEE TCAD, 1991); Kim, Lee and Markov, "SimPL: an effective placement algorithm" (ICCAD 2010).
