label: Golden and QoR differential tests for a placer
prereqs: The placer's core and change surface
lesson:
# Golden and QoR differential tests for a placer

No change to a placer, whether a parameter, a plug-in or a core edit, should be promoted on faith. Golden tests prove that kernels compute what they should; QoR differential tests compare the changed placer with a baseline across a regression suite and prove that only the intended metrics moved, by the intended amounts. Writing the gates precisely is what makes agent-generated changes safe to accept.

## Golden tests for placer kernels

Golden tests check deterministic pieces against known answers: HPWL of hand-built nets, B2B weights, density of a small bin grid, the Abacus result on a three-cell row, the legality checker on legal and illegal examples, and the incremental wirelength delta against full recomputation for random moves. They run in seconds, so the harness runs them after every edit. For a change at a seam, the plug-in's own golden tests join the suite. Determinism is a precondition: with fixed seeds and ordered reductions, the same input must give bit-identical output, otherwise a golden mismatch cannot be told apart from noise.

## Measuring QoR change

A QoR comparison runs the baseline and the changed placer on the same designs with the same downstream flow and reports metric changes. The basic number is the percent change: HPWL from 458000 to 455000 um is $-0.66\%$. A suite summary uses the geometric mean of new-over-baseline ratios, which treats a 1% change on a small design and on a large one equally and keeps one large design from dominating; for ratios 0.99, 1.01 and 0.97, the geometric mean is about 0.9899. Metrics include HPWL, overflow, legalization displacement, routed wirelength and DRC count where available, timing (WNS, TNS) and runtime, since a QoR gain that doubles runtime may not be acceptable.

## Promotion gates

A gate turns measurements into a decision. A typical one: on every regression design, HPWL may grow by at most 1% over baseline, overflow must stay at most 0.1, legality must hold, and runtime may grow by at most 10%. The change is blocked if any design fails, and the report lists which designs and metrics broke. For a targeted change, such as a rule plug-in, the gate also checks that the intended effect appears on the target design. Gates should be strict enough to catch regressions and loose enough to tolerate run-to-run noise, which is measured by running the baseline several times. Every promoted change is versioned and reversible, so a regression found later can be traced and rolled back.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum, section on verification of engine changes; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts metrics and regression documentation.

problems.q: A placer change is run on a reference design: baseline HPWL 313000 um, new HPWL 318634 um. What is the HPWL change, in percent (negative is better)? Round to 2 decimal places.
A placer change is run on a reference design: baseline HPWL 341000 um, new HPWL 347820 um. What is the HPWL change, in percent (negative is better)? Round to 2 decimal places.

A placer plug-in is promoted only if, on every regression design, HPWL grows by no more than 1% over baseline and final overflow is at most 0.1. label: Fast placement inside a modeling loop
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast placement inside a modeling loop

Placement exists in fast and accurate forms: a GPU global placer with loose stopping rules and RUDY congestion, versus full global and detailed placement followed by global routing. An agent exploring floorplans or parameters runs the fast version in a loop, uses its metrics and their error to decide which candidates deserve the accurate version, and bases final decisions only on accurate results.

## What the fast placer trades away

A fast placer stops at a higher overflow, uses coarser bins, skips or shortens detailed placement and estimates congestion with RUDY instead of a router. It returns HPWL, overflow and a congestion map in a fraction of the time, with a known error relative to the accurate flow. That error must be measured, not assumed: run both on a sample of designs and record the spread of the ratio, for example HPWL within about 3%. The fast placer must also be deterministic and seedable, so that differences between candidates come from the candidates rather than from noise, and its error should be re-measured whenever the design family changes.

## Deciding what to run accurately

Given fast estimates and an error band of $\pm e$, a candidate can be discarded only if even its optimistic value, estimate times $(1 - e)$, is worse than the best candidate's pessimistic value, best estimate times $(1 + e)$. With estimates 934, 910, 905, 990, 1059, 952, 1048 and 944 mm and $e = 2\%$, the best pessimistic value is 923.1 and only candidates whose optimistic value is at most that survive: 905, 910 and 934, three candidates for the accurate placer. If many candidates survive, the error band is too wide for the decision and the agent needs a better fast model or more accurate runs. Metric variance across seeds plays the same role as the error band.

## Pitfalls of the loop

An agent rewarded on fast-placer metrics can learn to exploit the fast model's blind spots, for example floorplans whose RUDY estimate looks clean but whose real routing congests near macros, a form of reward hacking. Guards include adding routability terms that correlate with the accurate flow, periodic accurate audits of chosen candidates, and making final decisions only from accurate results. Speed shifts the bottleneck: when global placement takes a minute, I/O, legalization and evaluation dominate, so the loop is only as fast as its slowest stage. The fast placer, its error model and the selection rule together form a skill whose manifest should state when its estimates can be trusted.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum, section on fast and accurate engines in a continuous loop; Lin et al., "DREAMPlace" (DAC 2019), on GPU placement speed.

problems.q:
In a fast-and-accurate loop, what is the fast placer's output used for?

A) Replacing the router

B) Tape-out

C) Ranking candidates and estimating metrics so the agent can decide what to run accurately

D) Final signoff
problems.a: Ranking candidates and estimating metrics so the agent can decide what to run accurately
problems.e: Fast results guide decisions; accurate runs confirm the chosen candidates.

problems.q:
Which metric is a natural fast-loop output of a placer?

A) Signoff DRC count

B) Silicon yield

C) Post-route parasitics

D) Estimated HPWL, overflow and a RUDY congestion map
problems.a: Estimated HPWL, overflow and a RUDY congestion map
problems.e: These are cheap to compute after global placement and correlate with final quality.

problems.q:
What does a fast placer typically trade away to run inside a modeling loop?

A) The ability to read DEF

B) Determinism, always

C) Accuracy: fewer iterations, coarser bins or skipped detailed placement

D) Legality of the netlist
problems.a: Accuracy: fewer iterations, coarser bins or skipped detailed placement
problems.e: Fast modes stop earlier and approximate more, giving estimates rather than final QoR.

problems.q:
An agent explores 7 floorplan variants with a fast placer whose HPWL is known to be within 3% of the accurate placer's. The fast HPWL estimates (mm) are 977, 1087, 948, 1078, 1097, 961, 1086. A variant can be discarded only if even its most optimistic true HPWL is worse than the best variant's most pessimistic one. How many variants must the agent re-run with the accurate placer?

A) 4 variants

B) 7 variants

C) 1 variant

D) 3 variants
problems.a: 3 variants
problems.e: The best estimate is 948, whose pessimistic value is 976.44. A variant survives if its optimistic value, estimate x 0.97, is at most that: 3 do.

problems.q:
An agent explores 7 floorplan variants with a fast placer whose HPWL is known to be within 5% of the accurate placer's. The fast HPWL estimates (mm) are 1043, 1009, 993, 1084, 1066, 931, 1012. A variant can be discarded only if even its most optimistic true HPWL is worse than the best variant's most pessimistic one. How many variants must the agent re-run with the accurate placer?

A) 4 variants

B) 7 variants

C) 5 variants

D) 1 variant
problems.a: 4 variants
problems.e: The best estimate is 931, whose pessimistic value is 977.55. A variant survives if its optimistic value, estimate x 0.95, is at most that: 4 do.

problems.q:
An agent explores 7 floorplan variants with a fast placer whose HPWL is known to be within 2% of the accurate placer's. The fast HPWL estimates (mm) are 958, 992, 908, 1033, 971, 902, 997. A variant can be discarded only if even its most optimistic true HPWL is worse than the best variant's most pessimistic one. How many variants must the agent re-run with the accurate placer?

A) 2 variants

B) 7 variants

C) 3 variants

D) 1 variant
problems.a: 2 variants
problems.e: The best estimate is 902, whose pessimistic value is 920.04. A variant survives if its optimistic value, estimate x 0.98, is at most that: 2 do.

problems.q:
Why must the fast placer be deterministic and seedable for the loop to work well?

A) So it uses less memory

B) So differences between candidates come from the candidates, not from run-to-run noise

C) So it can be used for signoff

D) So it never needs updating
problems.a: So differences between candidates come from the candidates, not from run-to-run noise
problems.e: Reproducible runs make comparisons and replay possible.

problems.q:
A GPU global placer cuts a run from 30 minutes to 1 minute. What does that change for an agent?

A) Nothing, agents do not use placers

B) It guarantees better QoR

C) It can explore about 30 variants in the time one used to take, if the rest of the evaluation is also fast

D) It makes routing unnecessary
problems.a: It can explore about 30 variants in the time one used to take, if the rest of the evaluation is also fast
problems.e: Faster engines widen the exploration budget; the end-to-end evaluation must keep up.
